summary:
The United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: trans visitors use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how to lawfully enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The preceding hearing had been told by the challengers that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. Any visitor arrested in the United Kingdom should therefore expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.
tangentialFactors:
TransActual UK's Gendered Spaces Report 2025 surveyed trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents and recorded their fears of harassment by those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces, evidence that the enforcement climate in practice runs ahead of what the statutory code alone conveys. Sex Matters, the campaign group behind the litigation, publicly welcomed the British Transport Police search-policy change, and its director Maya Forstater described the August 2026 code as practical and the law as clear, indicating organised advocacy sustaining the restrictive interpretation.

Northern Ireland sits on a separate equality-law footing and its Equality Commission was still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling as of August 2026, so the code's application there is not settled in the same way as in England, Wales and Scotland.
localsOnly:
For residents, the litigation concerns the statutory scaffolding rather than the direction of the outcome: the Outer House's judgment turned on Equality Act 2010 Schedule 22(1), the Prison Rules, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and the court's Article 8 analysis, and the Scottish Prison Service's guidance was non-statutory, which is why it fell. Scottish prisoners are now held by sex at birth absent a fresh lawful basis, with the risk-assessment route argued by government lawyers still available case by case.

Residents in custody face the same search rule as visitors: Police Scotland applies biological sex to any search involving more than outer clothing, and requests for an officer of a person's lived gender are accommodated where practicable. TransActual's report documents how these rules are experienced by UK residents in everyday gendered spaces, including harassment reported by survey respondents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Surrey Police's FOI-released searching/biological-sex policy (a Surrey and Sussex document) could not be retrieved at research time because the source returned HTTP 403; its contents are therefore unverified here and no claim in this record rests on it.

Whether the interim search policies issued by British Transport Police and Police Scotland have been made permanent, or replaced by a national consolidated policy, is not sourced in this inventory. The inventory also does not record whether the Scottish Prison Service issued replacement custody guidance after the 19 June 2026 ruling, nor whether the reported revisions to the Equality Act 2010 have been enacted in the form the UN experts criticised.
